body.p: The symmetric setting considers two parties who share a key and will use this key to imbue communicated data with various security attributes. The main security goals are privacy and authenticity of the communicated data. The present chapter looks at privacy. A later chapter looks at authenticity. Chapters 3 and 4 describe tools we shall use here.

sec.title: 5.1 Symmetric encryption schemes
sec.p: The primitive we will consider is called an encryption scheme. Such a scheme specifies an encryption algorithm, which tells the sender how to process the plaintext using the key, thereby producing the ciphertext that is actually transmitted. An encryption scheme also specifies a decryption algorithm, which tells the receiver how to retrieve the original plaintext from the transmission while possibly performing some verification, too. Finally, there is a key-generation algorithm, which produces a key that the parties need to share. The formal description follows.
Definition 5.1 A symmetric encryption scheme SE = (K, E, D) consists of three algorithms, as follows:

list-item.p: The randomized key generation algorithm K returns a string K. We let Keys(SE) denote the set of all strings that have non-zero probability of being output by K. The members of this set are called keys. We write K ←$ K for the operation of executing K and letting K denote the key returned.

The encryption algorithm E, which might be randomized or stateful, takes a key K ∈ Keys(SE) and a plaintext M ∈ {0,1}∗ to return a ciphertext C ∈ {0,1}∗ ∪ {⊥}. We write C ←$ EK(M) for the operation of executing E on K and M and letting C denote the ciphertext returned.

The deterministic decryption algorithm D takes a key K ∈ Keys(SE) and a ciphertext C ∈ {0,1}∗ to return some M ∈ {0,1}∗ ∪ {⊥}. We write M ← DK(C) for the operation of executing D on K and C and letting M denote the message returned.

sec.p: The scheme is said to provide correct decryption if for any key K ∈ Keys(SE), any sequence of messages M1,...,Mq ∈ {0,1}∗, and any sequence of ciphertexts Ci ←$ EK(Mi) that may arise in encrypting M1,...,Mq, it is the case that DK(Ci) = Mi for each Ci ≠ ⊥.

The key-generation algorithm, as the definition indicates, is randomized. It takes no inputs. When it is run, it flips coins internally and uses these to select a key K. Typically, the key is just a random string of some length, in which case this length is called the key length of the scheme.

The encryption algorithm may be either randomized or stateful. If randomized, it flips coins and uses those to compute its output on a given input K, M. Each time the algorithm is invoked, it flips coins anew. We say the encryption algorithm is stateful if its operation depends on a quantity called the state that is initialized in some pre-specified way. Usually, when there is state to be maintained, the state is just a counter. If there is no state maintained by the encryption algorithm the encryption scheme is said to be stateless.
In a stateless scheme, there is typically a set of strings M, called the plaintext space, such that M ∈ M iff Pr[K ←$ K; C ←$ EK(M): C ≠ ⊥] = 1.

The correct decryption requirement simply says that decryption works: if a message M is encrypted under a key K to yield a ciphertext C, then one can recover M by decrypting C under K. This holds, however, only if C ≠ ⊥.

sec.title: 5.2 Some symmetric encryption schemes
sec.p: We now provide a few examples of encryption schemes. We stress that not all of the schemes that follow are secure encryption schemes. Some are secure and some are not, as we will see later. All the schemes here satisfy the correct decryption requirement.

sec.title: 5.2.1 The one-time-pad encryption scheme
sec.p: Scheme 5.2 [One-time-pad encryption] The one-time-pad encryption scheme SE = (K, E, D) is stateful and deterministic. The key-generation algorithm simply returns a random k-bit string K, where the key-length k is a parameter of the scheme, so that the key space is Keys(SE) = {0,1}k. The encryptor maintains a counter ctr which is initially zero. The encryption and decryption algorithms operate as follows:

disp-quote.p:
algorithm EK(M)
Let static ctr ← 0
Let m ← |M|
if ctr + m > k then return ⊥
C ← M ⊕ K[ctr+1 .. ctr+m]
ctr ← ctr + m
return ⟨ctr−m, C⟩
algorithm DK(⟨ctr, C⟩)
Let m ← |M|
if ctr + m > k then return ⊥
M ← C ⊕ K[ctr+1 .. ctr+m]
return M

sec.p: Here X[i .. j] denotes the i-th through j-th bits of the binary string X. By ⟨ctr, C⟩ we mean a string that encodes the number ctr and the string C. The encryption algorithm XORs the message bits with key bits, starting with the key bit indicated by one plus the current counter value. The counter is then incremented by the length of the message. Key bits are not reused, and thus if not enough key bits are available to encrypt a message, the encryption algorithm returns ⊥. The ciphertext returned includes the value of the counter to enable decryption.

sec.title: 5.2.2 Some modes of operation
sec.p: The following schemes rely either on a family of permutations (i.e., a blockcipher) or a family of functions. Effectively, the mechanisms spell out how to use the blockcipher to encrypt. We call such a mechanism a mode of operation of the blockcipher. For some of the schemes it is convenient to assume that the length of the message to be encrypted is a positive multiple of a block length n. Accordingly, the encryption algorithm returns ⊥ if this is not the case.
The first scheme we consider is ECB (Electronic Codebook Mode).

Scheme 5.3 [ECB mode] Let E: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a blockcipher. Operating it in ECB (Electronic Code Book) mode yields a stateless symmetric encryption scheme SE = (K, E, D). The key-generation algorithm picks a random string K ←$ K and returns it. The encryption and decryption algorithms are depicted in Fig. 5.1.

disp-quote.p:
algorithm EK(M)
if (|M| mod n ≠ 0 or |M| = 0) then return ⊥
Break M into n-bit blocks M[1]···M[m]
for i ← 1 to m do
C[i] ← EK(M[i])
C ← C[1]···C[m]
return C
algorithm DK(C)
if (|C| mod n ≠ 0 or |C| = 0) then return ⊥
Break C into n-bit blocks C[1]···C[m]
for i ← 1 to m do
M[i] ← EK−1(C[i])
M ← M[1]···M[m]
return M

sec.p: The next scheme, cipher-block chaining (CBC) with random initial vector, is the most popular block-cipher mode of operation, used pervasively in practice.

Scheme 5.4 [CBC$ mode] Let E: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a blockcipher. Operating it in CBC mode with random IV yields a stateless symmetric encryption scheme, SE = (K, E, D). The key generation algorithm simply returns a random key for the blockcipher, K ←$ K. The encryption and decryption algorithms are depicted in Fig. 5.2. The IV (“initialization vector”) is C[0], which is chosen at random by the encryption algorithm, independently each time the algorithm is invoked.

disp-quote.p:
algorithm EK(M)
if (|M| mod n ≠ 0 or |M| = 0) then return ⊥
Break M into n-bit blocks M[1]···M[m]
C[0] ← IV ←$ {0,1}n
for i ← 1 to m do
C[i] ← EK(C[i−1] ⊕ M[i])
C ← C[1]···C[m]
return ⟨IV, C⟩
algorithm DK(⟨IV, C⟩)
if (|C| mod n ≠ 0 or |M| = 0) then return ⊥
Break C into n-bit blocks C[1]···C[m]
C[0] ← IV
for i ← 1 to m do
M[i] ← EK−1(C[i]) ⊕ C[i−1]
M ← M[1]···M[m]
return M

sec.p: For the following schemes it is useful to introduce some notation. If n ≥ 1 and i ≥ 0 are integers then we let [i]n denote the n-bit string that is the binary representation of integer i mod 2n.

Scheme 5.5 [CBCC mode] Let E: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a blockcipher. Operating it in CBC mode with counter IV yields a stateful symmetric encryption scheme, SE = (K, E, D). The key generation algorithm simply returns a random key for the blockcipher, K ←$ K. The encryptor maintains a counter ctr which is initially zero. The encryption and decryption algorithms are depicted in Fig. 5.3. The IV is set to the current value of the counter. The counter is then incremented each time a message is encrypted.

disp-quote.p:
algorithm EK(M)
static ctr ← 0
if (|M| mod n ≠ 0 or |M| = 0) then return ⊥
Break M into n-bit blocks M[1]···M[m]
if ctr ≥ 2n then return ⊥
C[0] ← IV ← [ctr]n
for i ← 1 to m do
C[i] ← EK(C[i−1] ⊕ M[i])
C ← C[1]···C[m]
ctr ← ctr + 1
return ⟨IV, C⟩

sec.p: The CTR (counter) modes that follow are not much used but perhaps wrongly so. We will see later that they have good privacy properties. In contrast to CBC, the encryption procedure is parallelizable, which can be exploited to speed up the process in the presence of hardware support. It is also the case that the methods work for strings of arbitrary bit lengths, without doing anything “special” to achieve this end.

Scheme 5.6 [CTR$ mode] Let F: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a family of functions (possibly a blockcipher, but not necessarily). Then CTR mode over F with a random starting point is a probabilistic, stateless symmetric encryption scheme, SE = (K, E, D). The encryption and decryption algorithms are depicted in Fig. 5.4. The starting point R is a random n-bit string used to define a sequence of values on which FK is applied to produce a “pseudo one-time pad” to which the plaintext is XORed. The starting point R is included in the ciphertext to enable decryption.

caption.p: CTR$ mode using a family of functions F: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n. This version of counter mode is randomized and stateless.

disp-quote.p:
algorithm EK(M)
m ← ⌈|M|/n⌉
R ←$ {0,1}n
Pad ← FK(R+0) ‖ FK(R+1) ‖ ··· ‖ FK(R+m−1)
Pad ← the first |M| bits of Pad
return C ← ⟨R, C′⟩
algorithm DK(⟨R, C′⟩)
m ← ⌈|C′|/n⌉
Pad ← FK(R) ‖ FK(R+1) ‖ ··· ‖ FK(R+m−1)
Pad ← the first |C′| bits of Pad
M ← C′ ⊕ Pad
return M

sec.p: Scheme 5.7 [CTRC mode] Let F: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a family of functions (possibly a blockcipher, but not necessarily). Operating it in CTR mode with a counter starting point is a stateful symmetric encryption scheme, SE = (K, E, D), which we call CTRC. The key-generation algorithm simply returns a random key for F. The encryptor maintains a counter ctr which is initially zero. The encryption and decryption algorithms are depicted in Fig. 5.5. Position index ctr is not allowed to wrap around: the encryption algorithm returns ⊥ if this would happen. The position index is included in the ciphertext to enable decryption.

caption.p: CTRC mode using a family of functions F: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n. This version of counter mode uses stateful (but deterministic) encryption.

disp-quote.p:
algorithm EK(M)
static ctr ← 0
m ← ⌈|M|/n⌉
If ctr + m − 1 ≥ 2n then return ⊥
Pad ← FK(ctr+0) ‖ FK(ctr+1) ‖ ··· ‖ FK(ctr+m−1)
Pad ← the first |M| bits of Pad
C ← M ⊕ Pad
ctr ← ctr + m
return ⟨ctr−m, C⟩
algorithm DK(⟨i, C⟩)
m ← ⌈|C|/n⌉
if i + m − 1 ≥ 2n then return ⊥
Pad ← FK(i+0) ‖ FK(i+1) ‖ ··· ‖ FK(i+m−1)
Pad ← the first |C| bits of Pad
M ← Pad ⊕ C
return M

sec.title: 5.3 Issues in privacy
sec.p: Let us fix a symmetric encryption scheme SE = (K, E, D). Two parties share a key K for this scheme, generated as K ←$ K. The adversary does not a priori know K. We now want to explore the issue of what the privacy of the scheme might mean.

The adversary is assumed able to capture any ciphertext that flows on the channel between the two parties. Our first question is: what exactly does “glean” mean? What tasks, were the adversary to accomplish them, would make us declare the scheme insecure?

For example, if the adversary can, from a few ciphertexts, derive the underlying key K, the scheme is definitely insecure. The mistake that is often made is to reverse this, saying that if key recovery is hard, then the scheme is secure. This is certainly not true, for the adversary might be able to figure out partial information about M—for example, the first bit, or the sum of all the bits—without recovering the key.

An important principle of good cryptographic design is that the encryption scheme should provide security regardless of the format of the plaintext. Users should not have to worry about how they format their data: they format it as they like, and encryption should provide privacy nonetheless.

At this point it should start becoming obvious that there is an infinite list of insecurity properties, and we can hardly attempt to characterize security as their absence. We need to think about security in a different and more direct way and arrive at some definition of it.

One might want to say something like: the encryption scheme is secure if given C, the adversary has no idea what M is. This however cannot be true because of what is called a priori information. Often something about the message is known before it is encrypted. We want schemes that are secure in the strongest possible natural sense.

What would an “ideal” encryption be like? It would be as though some angel took the message M from the sender and delivered it to the receiver, in some magic way. The adversary would see nothing at all. Intuitively, our goal is to approximate this as best as possible.

We do deviate from the ideal in one way: encryption is not asked to hide the length of the plaintext string. This information not only can leak but is usually supposed to be known to the adversary a priori.

Consider the ECB encryption scheme of Scheme 5.3. As an example of its failure: suppose a missile command center has just two messages, 1n for “fire” and 0n for “don’t fire.” When an adversary sees a ciphertext C1 and then observes a missile taking off, it knows the plaintext underlying C1. Thereafter, it can decrypt all subsequent messages by comparing them to C1.

In a secure encryption scheme, it should not be possible to relate ciphertexts of different messages of the same length in such a way that information is leaked. Not allowing message-equalities to be leaked has a dramatic implication: encryption must be probabilistic or depend on state information. If not, one can always tell if the same message was sent twice. Each encryption must use fresh coin tosses, or, say, a counter, and an encryption of a particular message may be different each time.

sec.title: 5.4.1 Definition
sec.p: The basic idea behind indistinguishability (or, more fully, left-or-right indistinguishability under a chosen-plaintext attack) is to consider an adversary (not in possession of the secret key) who chooses two messages of the same length. Then one of the two messages is encrypted, and the ciphertext is given to the adversary. The scheme is considered secure if the adversary has a hard time telling which of the two messages was the one encrypted.

We will actually give the adversary a little more power, letting it choose a whole sequence of pairs of equal-length messages. The adversary chooses a sequence of pairs (M0,1, M1,1),...,(M0,q, M1,q), where in each pair the two messages have the same length. We give to the adversary a sequence of ciphertexts C1,...,Cq where either (1) Ci is an encryption of M0,i for all 1 ≤ i ≤ q or (2) Ci is an encryption of M1,i for all 1 ≤ i ≤ q. The adversary must guess whether M0,1,...,M0,q were encrypted or M1,1,...,M1,q were encrypted.

To further empower the adversary, we let it choose the sequence of message pairs via a chosen plaintext attack: the adversary chooses the first pair, then receives C1, then chooses the second pair, receives C2, and so on.

We define the left-or-right encryption oracle (abbreviated lr-encryption oracle) EK(LR(·,·,b)) as shown in Fig. 5.6. The oracle encrypts one of the messages, the choice of which being made according to the bit b.

caption.p: Left-or-right (lor) encryption oracle used to define IND-CPA security of encryption scheme SE = (K, E, D).

disp-quote.p:
Oracle EK(LR(M0, M1, b)) // b ∈ {0,1} and M0, M1 ∈ {0,1}∗
if |M0| ≠ |M1| then return ⊥
C ←$ EK(Mb)
return C

sec.p: The two worlds are as follows. World 0: the oracle provided to the adversary is EK(LR(·,·,0)), so whenever the adversary makes a query (M0, M1) with |M0| = |M1|, the oracle computes C ←$ EK(M0), and returns C. World 1: the oracle provided to the adversary is EK(LR(·,·,1)), so the oracle computes C ←$ EK(M1), and returns C.
Definition 5.8 Let SE = (K, E, D) be a symmetric encryption scheme, and let A be an algorithm that has access to an oracle. We consider the following experiments:

disp-quote.p:
Experiment ExpSEind-cpa-1(A) Experiment ExpSEind-cpa-0(A)
K ←$ K K ←$ K
d ←$ AEK(LR(·,·,1)) d ←$ AEK(LR(·,·,0))
Return d Return d

sec.p: The IND-CPA advantage of A is defined as

disp-quote.p: AdvSEind-cpa(A) = Pr[ExpSEind-cpa-1(A) = 1] − Pr[ExpSEind-cpa-0(A) = 1].

sec.p: If AdvSEind-cpa(A) is small (meaning close to zero), it means that A is outputting 1 about as often in world 0 as in world 1, meaning it is not doing a good job of telling which world it is in. If this quantity is large (meaning close to one—or at least far from zero) then the adversary A is doing well, meaning our scheme SE is not secure.

Informally, for symmetric encryption scheme SE to be secure against chosen plaintext attack, the IND-CPA advantage of an adversary must be small, no matter what strategy the adversary tries. The technical notion is called left-or-right indistinguishability under chosen-plaintext attack, denoted IND-CPA.

sec.title: 5.4.2 Alternative interpretation
sec.p: We can view the task of the adversary as trying to guess which world it is in. A trivial guess is for the adversary to return a random bit, giving probability 1/2 of being right. The advantage of the adversary measures how much better than this it does at guessing which world it is in, namely the excess over 1/2 of the adversary’s probability of guessing correctly.
Proposition 5.9 Let SE = (K, E, D) be a symmetric encryption scheme, and let A be an algorithm that has access to an oracle. We consider the following experiment:

disp-quote.p:
Experiment ExpSEind-cpa-cg(A)
b ←$ {0,1}; K ←$ K
b′ ←$ AEK(LR(·,·,b))
if b′ = b then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: Then AdvSEind-cpa(A) = 2 · Pr[ExpSEind-cpa-cg(A) = 1] − 1.

In the above experiment, adversary A is run with an oracle for world b, where the bit b is chosen at random. A eventually outputs a bit b′, its guess as to the value of b. The experiment returns 1 if A’s guess is correct. The “advantage” of A can be viewed as the excess of the correct-guess probability over 1/2, which re-scaled equals AdvSEind-cpa(A).

Proof of Proposition 5.9: The claim follows by a straightforward calculation via standard conditioning on the value of b. One observes that the conditional probabilities Pr[b′ = 1 | b = 1] and Pr[b′ = 1 | b = 0] are exactly the probabilities that A returns 1 in the experiments of Definition 5.8.

sec.title: 5.4.3 Why is this a good definition?
sec.p: Our thesis is that we should consider an encryption scheme to be “secure” if and only if it is IND-CPA secure, meaning that the above formalization captures our intuitive sense of privacy. A test of our definition is that it implies the necessary properties we have discussed—security against key-recovery, against plaintext-recovery, and more. We will prove such things later. For now, let us continue to get a better sense of how to work with the definition by using it to show that certain schemes are insecure.

sec.title: 5.5 Example chosen-plaintext attacks
sec.p: We illustrate the use of our IND-CPA definition in finding attacks by providing an attack on ECB mode, and also a general attack on deterministic, stateless schemes.

sec.title: 5.5.1 Attack on ECB
sec.p: Let us fix a blockcipher E: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n. The ECB symmetric encryption scheme SE = (K, E, D) was described as Scheme 5.3. Notice that if two plaintexts M and M′ agree in the first block, then so do the corresponding ciphertexts. So an adversary, given the ciphertexts, can tell whether or not the first blocks of the corresponding plaintexts are the same. This is loss of partial information about the plaintexts. We construct the following adversary A:

disp-quote.p:
Adversary AEK(LR(·,·,b))
M0 ← 02n; M1 ← 0n ‖ 1n
C[1]C[2] ← EK(LR(M0, M1, b))
If C[1] = C[2] then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: We claim that Pr[ExpSEind-cpa-1(A) = 1] = 1 and Pr[ExpSEind-cpa-0(A) = 1] = 0. In world 1, the oracle returns C[1]C[2] = EK(0n) ‖ EK(0n), so C[1] = C[2] and A returns 1. In world 0, the oracle returns EK(0n)EK(1n). Since E is a permutation, C[1] ≠ C[2], so A returns 0. Subtracting, AdvSEind-cpa(A) = 1 − 0 = 1. And A achieved this advantage by making just one oracle query of length 2n bits. This means the ECB encryption scheme is insecure.

There is an important feature of this attack that must be emphasized: ECB is an insecure encryption scheme even if the underlying blockcipher E is highly secure. The weakness is not in the tool being used (here the blockcipher) but in the manner we are using it. It is the ECB mechanism that is at fault. Even the best of tools are useless if you don’t know how to properly use them.

sec.title: 5.5.2 Any deterministic, stateless scheme is insecure
sec.p: ECB mode is deterministic and stateless, so that if the same message is encrypted twice, the same ciphertext is returned. It turns out that this property, in general, results in an insecure scheme.

Proposition 5.10 Let SE = (K, E, D) be a deterministic, stateless symmetric encryption scheme. Assume there is an integer m such that the plaintext space of the scheme contains two distinct strings of length m. Then there is an adversary A such that AdvSEind-cpa(A) = 1. Adversary A runs in time O(m) and asks just two queries, each of length m.
Proof of Proposition 5.10: Our adversary works like this:

disp-quote.p:
Adversary Af
Let X, Y be distinct, m-bit strings in the plaintext space
C1 ← EK(LR(X, Y, b))
C2 ← EK(LR(Y, Y, b))
If C1 = C2 then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: In world 1, the oracle returns C1 = EK(Y) and C2 = EK(Y), and since the encryption function is deterministic and stateless, C1 = C2, so A returns 1. In world 0, the oracle returns C1 = EK(X) and C2 = EK(Y), and since it is required that decryption be able to recover the message, it must be that C1 ≠ C2, so A returns 0. Subtracting, AdvSEind-cpa(A) = 1 − 0 = 1.

sec.title: 5.5.3 Attack on CBC encryption with counter IV
sec.p: Let us fix a blockcipher E: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n. Let SE = (K, E, D) be the corresponding counter-based version of the CBC encryption mode described in Scheme 5.5. We show that this scheme is insecure. The reason is that the adversary can predict the counter value. Our adversary works like this:

disp-quote.p:
Adversary AEK(LR(·,·,b))
M0,1 ← 0n; M1,1 ← 0n
M0,2 ← 0n; M1,2 ← 0n−11
⟨IV1, C1⟩ ←$ EK(LR(M0,1, M1,1, b))
⟨IV2, C2⟩ ←$ EK(LR(M0,2, M1,2, b))
If C1 = C2 then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: In world 0, IV1 = 0 and IV2 = 1 and C1 = EK(0) and C2 = EK(1), so C1 ≠ C2 and the experiment returns 0. In world 1, IV1 = 0 and IV2 = 1 and C1 = EK(0) and C2 = EK(0), so the experiment returns 1. Subtracting, AdvSEind-cpa(A) = 1 − 0 = 1, showing that A has a very high advantage. So the scheme is insecure.

sec.title: 5.6 Semantic security
sec.p: In this section we describe an alternative notion of encryption-scheme security, semantic security, again under a chosen-plaintext attack (abbreviated SEM-CPA). It captures the idea that a secure encryption scheme should hide all information about an unknown plaintext. We then show that IND-CPA implies SEM-CPA.

Semantic security was introduced by Goldwasser and Micali for public-key encryption. It transfers the intuition of Shannon’s notion of security to a setting where security is not absolute but dependent on the computational effort made by an adversary. Shannon says that an encryption scheme is secure if that which can be determined about a plaintext from its ciphertext can be determined in the absence of the ciphertext. Semantic security asks that that which can be efficiently computed about some plaintexts from their ciphertexts can be computed, just as easily, in the absence of those ciphertexts.
Definition 5.11 [Semantic security] Let SE = (K, E, D) be a symmetric encryption scheme, and let A be an algorithm that has access to an oracle. We consider the following experiments:

disp-quote.p:
Experiment ExpSEss-cpa-1(A) Experiment ExpSEss-cpa-0(A)
K ←$ K, s ←$ ε K ←$ K, s ←$ ε
for i ← 1 to q do for i ← 1 to q do
(Mi, s) ←$ A(s) (Mi, s) ←$ A(s)
Mi, Mi′ ←$ Mi Mi, Mi′ ←$ Mi
Ci ←$ EK(Mi), ... Ci ←$ EK(Mi′), ...
(f, Y) ←$ A(s) (f, Y) ←$ A(s)
return f(M1,...,Mq) = Y return f(M1,...,Mq) = Y

sec.p: The SEM-CPA advantage of A is defined as

disp-quote.p: AdvSEsem-cpa(A) = Pr[ExpSEss-cpa-1(A) ⇒ 1] − Pr[ExpSEss-cpa-0(A) ⇒ 1].

sec.p: In the definition, each experiment initializes by choosing a random key K. A total of q times, the adversary chooses a message space Mi. Two random samples Mi and Mi′ are drawn from this message space. The encryption of one of these messages is returned to the adversary: Mi for experiment 1 and Mi′ for experiment 0. By f we denote a deterministic function. By Y we denote a string. The string s represents saved state. The adversary is given the ability to choose the message spaces, to choose the partial information about the messages it finds convenient to predict, and to be fully adaptive.

Theorem 5.12 [IND-CPA ⇒ SEM-CPA] Let SE = (K, E, D) be a symmetric encryption scheme and let A be an adversary (for attacking the SEM-CPA security of SE) that runs in time at most t and asks at most q queries, these queries totaling at most μ bits. Then there exists an adversary B (for attacking the IND-CPA security of SE) that achieves advantage AdvSEind-cpa(B) ≥ AdvSEsem-cpa(A) and where B runs in time t + O(μ) and asks at most q queries, these queries totaling μ bits.
Proof: The adversary B, which has oracle g, is constructed as follows:

disp-quote.p:
algorithm Bg
s ←$ ε
for i ← 1 to q do
(Mi, s) ←$ A(s)
Mi, Mi′ ←$ Mi
if |Mi| ≠ |Mi′| then Mi ← Mi′ ← ε
Ci ← g(Mi′, Mi), s ← ⟨s, Ci⟩
(f, Y) ←$ A(s)
if f(M1,...,Mq) = Y then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: If g is instantiated by a right encryption oracle (returning C ←$ EK(M) in response to a query (M′, M)), then the algorithm above coincides with experiment ExpSEss-cpa-1(A). If g is instantiated by a left encryption oracle (returning C ←$ EK(M′) in response to a query (M′, M)), then the algorithm above coincides with experiment ExpSEss-cpa-0(A). It follows that AdvSEsem-cpa(B) = AdvSEind-cpa(A).

sec.title: 5.7 Security of CTR modes
sec.p: Recall that the CTR (counter) mode of operation of a family of functions comes in two variants: the randomized (stateless) version CTRC of Scheme 5.6, and the counter-based (stateful) mechanism CTR$ of Scheme 5.7. Both modes achieve indistinguishability under a chosen-plaintext attack, but the quantitative security is a little different.

Theorem 5.13 [Security of CTRC mode] Let F: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a family of functions and let SE = (K, E, D) be the corresponding CTRC symmetric encryption scheme as described in Scheme 5.7. Let A be an adversary (for attacking the IND-CPA security of SE) that runs in time at most t and asks at most q queries, these totaling at most σ n-bit blocks. Then there exists an adversary B (attacking the PRF security of F) such that

disp-quote.p: AdvSEind-cpa(A) ≤ AdvFprf(B).

sec.p: Furthermore B runs in time at most t′ = t + O(q + nσ) and asks at most q′ = σ oracle queries.

Theorem 5.14 [Security of CTR$ mode] Let F: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a blockcipher and let SE = (K, E, D) be the corresponding CTR$ symmetric encryption scheme as described in Scheme 5.6. Let A be an adversary (for attacking the IND-CPA security of SE) that runs in time at most t and asks at most q queries, these totaling at most σ n-bit blocks. Then there exists an adversary B (attacking the PRF security of F) such that

disp-quote.p: AdvSEind-cpa(A) ≤ AdvFprf(B) + 0.5σ2 / 2n.

sec.p: Furthermore B runs in time at most t′ = t + O(q + nσ) and asks at most q′ = σ oracle queries.

The above theorems exemplify the kinds of results that the provable-security approach is about: we are able to provide provable guarantees of security of some higher level cryptographic construct (in this case, a symmetric encryption scheme) based on the assumption that some building block (in this case an underlying function family) is secure. They are saying that CTR mode does not have design flaws. They are saying that as long as you use a good blockcipher, you are assured that nobody will break your encryption scheme.

Example 5.15 Let us suppose that F is the blockcipher AES, so that n = 128. Suppose I want to encrypt q = 230 messages, each being one kilobyte (213 bits) long. I am thus encrypting a total of σ = 236 blocks. Theorem 5.14 says that there exists a B satisfying the stated conditions. Under the assumption that the best attack on the PRF security of AES is a birthday attack, meaning B’s advantage is no more than q2 / 2128, we have that AdvSEind-cpa(A) is at most 1.5 · 272 / 2128 ≤ 1 / 255. This is a very small number, saying that our encryption is secure. Note however that if we encrypt 264 blocks of data, our provable-security bound becomes meaningless.

sec.title: 5.7.1 Proof of Theorem 5.13
sec.p: An important observation regarding the CTR scheme is that the encryption and decryption operations do not need direct access to the key K, but only access to a subroutine, or oracle, that implements the function FK. We introduce a scheme that takes as a parameter any given family of functions G having domain and range {0,1}n. Let SE[G] = (K, E, D) denote the symmetric encryption scheme defined as follows. The key generation algorithm simply returns a random instance of G; the encryption and decryption algorithms are shown in Fig. 5.7.

caption.p: Version SE[G] = (K, E, D) of the CTRC scheme parameterized by a family of functions G.

disp-quote.p:
algorithm Eg(M)
static ctr ← 0
m ← ⌈|M|/L⌉
If ctr + m − 1 ≥ 2n then return ⊥
Pad ← g(ctr) ‖ g(ctr+1) ‖ ··· ‖ g(ctr+m−1)
Pad ← the first |M| bits of Pad
C ← M ⊕ Pad
ctr ← ctr + m
return ⟨ctr−m, C⟩

sec.p: The scheme in which we are interested is SE[F] where F is our given family of functions. The proof breaks into two parts. The first step removes F from the picture and looks instead at an “idealized” version of the scheme: SE[Func(n, n)]. Here, a random function g of n-bits to n-bits is used where the original scheme would use FK.
Lemma 5.16 [Security of CTRC using a random function] Let A be any IND-CPA adversary attacking SE[Func(n, n)], where the scheme is depicted in Fig. 5.7. Then AdvSE[Func(n,n)]ind-cpa(A) = 0.

The lemma says the adversary has zero advantage, meaning no chance at all of breaking the scheme. The result is information-theoretic: it holds regardless of how much computing time the adversary invests. It is not true of all modes (ECB is insecure even with a random permutation).
Proof of Theorem 5.13: Let A be any IND-CPA adversary attacking SE = (K, E, D). There exists an adversary B such that

disp-quote.p: AdvSEind-cpa(A) ≤ 2 · AdvFprf(B). (5.1)

sec.p: Adversary B takes an oracle g: {0,1}n → {0,1}n and determines which world it is in by running A as a subroutine and simulating the lr-encryption oracle for A:

disp-quote.p:
Adversary Bg
b ←$ {0,1}
Run adversary A, replying to its oracle queries as follows:
When A makes an oracle query (M0, M1) do
C ←$ Eg(Mb)
Return C to A as the answer
Until A stops and outputs a bit b′
If b′ = b then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: Here Eg(·) denotes the encryption function of the generalized CTRC scheme defined in Fig. 5.7, which can be implemented given an oracle for g. Adversary B itself picks the challenge bit b representing the choice of worlds for A, and then sees whether or not A succeeds. If it does, B bets that g is an instance of F; otherwise, B bets that g is an instance of Func(n, n).

For the analysis: when B is in world 1, the encryption scheme from A’s point of view is SE[F]; when B is in world 0, the scheme from A’s point of view is SE[Func(n, n)]. Using the correct-guess interpretation of Proposition 5.9:

disp-quote.p:
Pr[ExpFprf-1(B) = 1] = 1/2 + (1/2) · AdvSE[F]ind-cpa(A) (5.2)
Pr[ExpFprf-0(B) = 1] = 1/2 + (1/2) · AdvSE[Func(n,n)]ind-cpa(A). (5.3)

sec.p: Subtracting and applying Lemma 5.16 (which gives AdvSE[Func(n,n)]ind-cpa(A) = 0) yields AdvFprf(B) = (1/2) · AdvSE[F]ind-cpa(A), and rearranging gives Equation (5.1).

Proof of Lemma 5.16: The intuition is simple. When g is a random function, its value on successive counter values yields a one-time pad, a truly random and unpredictable sequence of bits. The inputs to g are always distinct (they are consecutive counter values). The outputs of g are thus random and independent. Since the data is XORed to this sequence, the adversary gets no information whatsoever about it.

Formally, each cipher block satisfies: Ci[j] = g([m1 + ··· + mi−1 + j]l) ⊕ Mi,b[j]. The values on which g is applied are all distinct, so the outputs of g are all random and independent. Any given output sequence from the oracle is equally likely in both worlds. Since the adversary determines its output bit based on this output sequence, its probability of returning 1 must be the same in both worlds, so its IND-CPA advantage is zero.

sec.title: 5.7.2 Proof of Theorem 5.14
sec.p: The proof of Theorem 5.14 reuses a lot of what we did for the proof of Theorem 5.13. We first look at the scheme when g is a random function, and then use the pseudorandomness of the given family F to deduce the theorem. As before we associate to a family of functions G a parameterized version of the CTR$ scheme, SE[G] = (K, E, D). The encryption and decryption algorithms are shown in Fig. 5.8. Here is the main lemma.

caption.p: Version SE[G] = (K, E, D) of the CTR$ scheme parameterized by a family of functions G.

disp-quote.p:
algorithm Eg(M)
m ← ⌈|M|/n⌉
R ←$ {0,1}n
Pad ← g(R+0) ‖ g(R+1) ‖ ··· ‖ g(R+m−1)
Pad ← the first |M| bits of Pad
C′ ← M ⊕ Pad
C ← R ‖ C′
return C

sec.p: Lemma 5.17 [Security of CTR$ using a random function] Let A be any IND-CPA adversary attacking SE[Func(n, n)], where the scheme is depicted in Fig. 5.8. Then AdvSE[Func(n,n)]ind-cpa(A) ≤ 0.5σ2 / 2n, assuming A asks a number of queries whose total length is at most σ n-bit blocks.
The proof of Theorem 5.14 given this lemma is the subject of Problem 5.6. We now prove Lemma 5.17 using the following auxiliary probabilistic lemma.

Lemma 5.18 Let n, q be positive integers, and let m1,...,mq < 2n also be positive integers. Suppose we pick q integers r1,...,rq from [0..2n−1] uniformly and independently at random. We say that a collision occurs if some two (or more) numbers among all ri, ri+1, ..., ri+mi−1 (for i = 1,...,q, where addition is performed modulo 2n) are equal. Then

Proof of Lemma 5.18: Think of having 2n bins. We have q balls, and for each ball we choose a random bin ri. When we throw the i-th ball, we define a row ri, ri+1,...,ri+mi−1 in the table. A collision occurs if any value in a new row equals some value in a previous row. By conditioning on each step:

disp-quote.p: Pr[Col] ≤ ∑i=2q Pr[Coli | NoColi−1] ≤ ∑i=2q ((i−1)mi + mi−1 + ··· + m1) / 2n = (q−1)(m1 + ··· + mq) / 2n.

sec.p: The collision probability when throwing the i-th ball given no prior collision is at most the number of “forbidden” starting positions for ri, which is bounded by (i−1)mi + mi−1 + ··· + m1 − (i−1). Dropping the negative term gives Equation (5.6), and the total weight of each mi across the sum is q−1.
Proof of Lemma 5.17: The proof defines the event NoCol that the starting points r1,...,rq and their offsets produce a collision-free table. Three claims are established:

list-item.label: Claim 1:
list-item.p: Pr1[Col] = Pr0[Col]. (The probability of a collision does not depend on which world we are in, since the random values ri are chosen in exactly the same way in both worlds.)

list-item.label: Claim 2:
list-item.p: Pr0[A = 1 | NoCol] = Pr1[A = 1 | NoCol]. (Given NoCol, the function g is evaluated at distinct points each time; outputs are random and independent, making cipher blocks uniformly distributed regardless of the messages.)

list-item.label: Claim 3:
list-item.p: Pr0[Col] ≤ σ2 / 2n. (By Lemma 5.18, noting that m1 + ··· + mq = σ.)

sec.p: These three claims together give AdvSE[Func(n,n)]ind-cpa(A) = Pr1[A = 1] − Pr0[A = 1] ≤ Pr0[Col] ≤ σ2 / 2n. Dividing by 2 gives the stated bound of 0.5σ2 / 2n.

sec.title: 5.8 Security of CBC with a random IV
sec.p: In this section we show that CBC encryption using a random IV is IND-CPA secure as long as E is a blockcipher that is a secure PRF or PRP.

Theorem 5.19 [Security of CBC$ mode] Let E: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a blockcipher and let SE = (K, E, D) be the corresponding CBC$ symmetric encryption scheme as described in Scheme 5.4. Let A be an adversary (for attacking the IND-CPA security of SE) that runs in time at most t and asks at most q queries, these totaling at most σ n-bit blocks. Then there exists an adversary B (attacking the PRF security of E) such that

disp-quote.p: AdvSEind-cpa(A) ≤ AdvEprf(B) + σ2 / 2n.

sec.p: Furthermore B runs in time at most t′ = t + O(q + nσ) and asks at most q′ = σ oracle queries.

To prove this theorem we proceed as before to introduce a parameterized scheme SE[G] for any given family of functions G. The algorithms of the scheme are depicted in Fig. 5.9. Note that the decryption algorithm simply returns ⊥, so this scheme does not have the correct decryption property. But one can still discuss its security.

caption.p: Version SE[G] = (K, E, D) of the CBC$ scheme parameterized by a family of functions G.

disp-quote.p:
algorithm Eg(M)
if (|M| mod n ≠ 0 or |M| = 0) then return ⊥
Break M into n-bit blocks M[1]···M[m]
C[0] ← IV ←$ {0,1}n
for i ← 1 to m do
C[i] ← g(C[i−1] ⊕ M[i])
C ← C[1]···C[m]
return ⟨IV, C⟩
algorithm Dg(⟨IV, C⟩)
return ⊥

sec.p: Lemma 5.20 [Security of CBC$ using a random function] Let A be any IND-CPA adversary attacking SE[Func(n, n)], where the scheme is depicted in Fig. 5.9. Then

disp-quote.p: AdvCBC$[Func(n,n)]ind-cpa(A) ≤ σ2 / 2n,

sec.p: assuming A asks a number of queries whose total length is at most σ n-bit blocks.

Proof: Consider the three games specified in Fig. 5.10. Game C0 precisely imitates the encryption of the left message under a random function ρ. Game C1 precisely imitates the encryption of the right message under a random function ρ. Game C2 omits both shaded statements. Since games C0, C1, and C2 are identical-until-bad-is-set, the fundamental lemma of game playing gives us that

disp-quote.p: AdvCBC$[Func(n,n)]ind-cpa(A) ≤ Pr[AC2 sets bad].

sec.p: The domain of ρ starts off with zero points and grows one point at a time until it reaches at most σ − 1 points. Since each Xi = Mi ⊕ Ci−1 is random and independent of the current domain of ρ (because Ci−1 is chosen at random and is independent of everything previously computed), the probability that bad is set at line 14 is at most (1 + 2 + ··· + (σ−1)) / 2n. The same holds for line 15. Summing, the probability that bad is set in Game C2 is at most σ2 / 2n.

caption.p: Games used in the analysis of CBC$. Game C0 includes the first shaded statement but omits the second. It CBC$-encrypts M = M1···Mm. Game C1 includes the second shaded statement but omits the first. It CBC$-encrypts M′ = M1′···Mm′. Game C2 omits both shaded statements and is used in the analysis.

sec.p: Corollary 5.21 [Security of CBC$ using a blockcipher] Let n ≥ 1 be a number and let A be an adversary that queries at most σ blocks. Then

disp-quote.p: AdvCBC$[Perm(n)]ind-cpa(A) ≤ 2σ2 / 2n.

sec.p: Proof: Applying the Switching Lemma (Lemma 4.17) to Lemma 5.20, and bounding via the triangle inequality:

disp-quote.p: AdvCBC$[Perm(n)]ind-cpa(A) ≤ 0.5σ2/2n + σ2/2n + 0.5σ2/2n = 2σ2/2n.

sec.p: Corollary 5.22 [Security of CBC$ using a real blockcipher] Let n ≥ 1 and let E: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a blockcipher. Let A be an adversary (for attacking CBC$-encryption in the IND-CPA sense) that runs in time at most t and that queries at most σ blocks. Then there exists an adversary B (for attacking blockcipher E in the PRP-CPA sense) where

disp-quote.p: AdvEprp(B) ≥ AdvCBC$[E]ind-cpa(A) − 2σ2 / 2n

sec.p: and where B makes at most σ queries and runs in time at most t + O(nσ).

We have so far shown that the IND-CPA advantage of CBC$ falls off by an amount that is at most quadratic in the number of blocks σ asked by the adversary. We can also give a matching attack, showing that there actually is an adversary that obtains advantage of about σ2/2n.

Proposition 5.23 Let n ≥ 1, let E: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a function family, and let σ ∈ [0..√(2 · 2n/2−1)]. Then there is an adversary A that asks a single query consisting of σ blocks, runs in time O(nσ log(σ)), and achieves advantage

disp-quote.p: AdvCBC[E]ind-cpa(A) ≥ 0.15σ2/2n.

sec.p: The proof shows that when encrypting a random message R of σ blocks under a random IV, the resulting ciphertext is uniformly distributed. The birthday bound ensures collisions among the ciphertext blocks occur with probability at least 0.3σ2/2n. When a collision Ci = CI is found, the next blocks Ci+1 and CI+1 are equal when encrypting the left message (all zeros), but random and independent when encrypting the right message, yielding the stated advantage.

sec.title: 5.9 Indistinguishability under chosen-ciphertext attack
sec.p: So far we have considered privacy under chosen-plaintext attack. Sometimes we want to consider privacy when the adversary is capable of mounting a stronger type of attack, namely a chosen-ciphertext attack. In this type of attack, an adversary has access to a decryption oracle. It can feed this oracle a ciphertext and get back the corresponding plaintext.

If an adversary has access to a decryption oracle, security at first seems moot, since after all it can decrypt anything it wants. To create a meaningful notion of security, we put a restriction on the use of the decryption oracle. We call a query C to the decryption oracle illegitimate if C was previously returned by the lr-encryption oracle; otherwise a query is legitimate. We insist that only legitimate queries are allowed.

This restriction still leaves the adversary with a lot of power. Typically, a successful chosen-ciphertext attack proceeds by taking a ciphertext C returned by the lr-encryption oracle, modifying it into a related ciphertext C′, and querying the decryption oracle with C′. The attacker seeks to create C′ in such a way that its decryption tells the attacker what the underlying message M was.
Definition 5.24 Let SE = (K, E, D) be a symmetric encryption scheme, let A be an algorithm that has access to two oracles, and let b be a bit. We consider the following experiment:

disp-quote.p:
Experiment ExpSEind-cca-b(A)
K ←$ K
b ←$ AEK(LR(·,·,b)), DK(·)
If A queried DK(·) on a ciphertext previously returned by EK(LR(·,·,b)) then return 0 else return b

sec.p: The IND-CCA advantage of A is defined as

disp-quote.p: AdvSEind-cca(A) = Pr[ExpSEind-cca-1(A) = 1] − Pr[ExpSEind-cca-0(A) = 1].

sec.p: We consider an encryption scheme to be “secure against chosen-ciphertext attack” if a “reasonable” adversary cannot obtain “significant” advantage in distinguishing the cases b = 0 and b = 1 given access to the oracles. The technical notion is called indistinguishability under chosen-ciphertext attack, denoted IND-CCA.

sec.title: 5.10 Example chosen-ciphertext attacks
sec.p: Chosen-ciphertext attacks are powerful enough to break all the standard modes of operation, even those like CTR and CBC that are secure against chosen-plaintext attack.

sec.title: 5.10.1 Attacks on the CTR schemes
sec.p: Let F: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a family of functions and let SE = (K, E, D) be the associated CTR$ symmetric encryption scheme as described in Scheme 5.6. The weakness is the following: say ⟨r, C⟩ is a ciphertext of some n-bit message M, and we flip bit i of C, resulting in a new ciphertext ⟨r, C′⟩. Let M′ be the message obtained by decrypting the new ciphertext. Then M′ equals M with the i-th bit flipped. Thus, by making a decryption oracle query of ⟨r, C′⟩ one can learn M′ and thus M.

Proposition 5.25 Let F: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a family of functions and let SE = (K, E, D) be the corresponding CTR$ symmetric encryption scheme as described in Scheme 5.6. Then AdvSEind-cca(t, 1, n, 1, 2n) = 1 for t = O(n) plus the time for one application of F.
Proof of Proposition 5.25: We present adversary A with one query to each oracle and AdvSEind-cca(A) = 1:

disp-quote.p:
Adversary AEK(LR(·,·,b)), DK(·)
M0 ← 0n; M1 ← 1n
⟨r, C⟩ ← EK(LR(M0, M1, b))
C′ ← C ⊕ 1n
M ← DK(⟨r, C′⟩)
If M = M0 then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: The decryption query ⟨r, C′⟩ ≠ ⟨r, C⟩, so it is legitimate. In world 1 (b = 1), C = FK(r+1) ⊕ 1n, so M = DK(⟨r, C′⟩) = FK(r+1) ⊕ C′ = FK(r+1) ⊕ C ⊕ 1n = FK(r+1) ⊕ (FK(r+1) ⊕ 1n) ⊕ 1n = 0n = M0, so A returns 1. In world 0 (b = 0), C = FK(r+1) ⊕ 0n, so M = 1n = M1, so A returns 0. Hence AdvSEind-cca(A) = 1 − 0 = 1.

sec.title: 5.10.2 Attack on CBC$
sec.p: Let E: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a blockcipher and let SE = (K, E, D) be the associated CBC$ symmetric encryption scheme as described in Scheme 5.4. The weakness: say ⟨IV, C[1]⟩ is a ciphertext of some n-bit message M, and we flip bit i of the IV, resulting in a new ciphertext ⟨IV′, C[1]⟩. Let M′ be the message obtained by decrypting the new ciphertext. Then M′ equals M with the i-th bit flipped. Thus, by making a decryption oracle query of ⟨IV′, C[1]⟩ one can learn M′ and thus M.

Proposition 5.26 Let E: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a blockcipher and let SE = (K, E, D) be the corresponding CBC$ encryption scheme as described in Scheme 5.4. Then AdvSEind-cca(t, 1, n, 1, 2n) = 1 for t = O(n) plus the time for one application of F.
Proof of Proposition 5.26: We present adversary A with one query to each oracle and AdvSEind-cca(A) = 1:

disp-quote.p:
Adversary AEK(LR(·,·,b)), DK(·)
M0 ← 0n; M1 ← 1n
⟨IV, C[1]⟩ ← EK(LR(M0, M1, b))
IV′ ← IV ⊕ 1n
M ← DK(⟨IV′, C[1]⟩)
If M = M0 then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: The decryption query ⟨IV′, C[1]⟩ ≠ ⟨IV, C[1]⟩, so it is legitimate. In world 1 (b = 1), C[1] = EK(IV ⊕ 1n), so M = EK−1(C[1]) ⊕ IV′ = (IV ⊕ 1n) ⊕ (IV ⊕ 1n) = 0n = M0, so A returns 1. In world 0 (b = 0), C[1] = EK(IV ⊕ 0n), so M = EK−1(C[1]) ⊕ IV′ = (IV ⊕ 0n) ⊕ (IV ⊕ 1n) = 1n = M1, so A returns 0. Hence AdvSEind-cca(A) = 1 − 0 = 1.

sec.title: 5.11 Historical notes
sec.p: The pioneering work on the theory of encryption is that of Goldwasser and Micali, with refinements by others. This body of work is however in the asymmetric (i.e., public key) setting, and uses the asymptotic framework of polynomial-time adversaries and negligible success probabilities. The treatment of symmetric encryption we are using is from Bellare, Desai, Jokipii and Rogaway. In particular Definition 5.1 and the concrete security framework are from that work. The analysis of the CTR and CBC mode encryption schemes, as given in Theorems 5.13, 5.14 and 5.19, is also from that work.

sec.title: 5.12 Problems
sec.p: Problem 5.1 Formalize a notion of security against key-recovery for symmetric encryption schemes. Then prove that IND-CPA security implies key-recovery security.
Problem 5.2 Consider the following notion of indistinguishability of an encryption scheme SE = (K, E, D):

disp-quote.p: AdvSEind0-cpa(A) = Pr[K ←$ K : AEK(·) ⇒ 1] − Pr[K ←$ K : AEK(0|·|) ⇒ 1].

sec.p: That is, a scheme is IND0-CPA secure if the encryption of every string looks like the encryption of an equal number of zeros. Prove that this notion of security is equivalent to IND-CPA security, carefully stating a pair of theorems and proving them.

Problem 5.3 The definition above for IND0-CPA provides the adversary with no method to get, with certitude, the encryption of a given message. Consider providing the adversary an additional “reference” oracle that always encrypts the queried string. Consider defining the corresponding advantage notion in the natural way:

disp-quote.p: AdvSEind0-cpa*(A) = Pr[K ←$ K : AEK(·), EK(·) ⇒ 1] − Pr[K ←$ K : A0|M|, EK(·) ⇒ 1].

sec.p: State and prove a theorem that shows that this notion of security is equivalent to our original IND0-CPA notion (and therefore to IND-CPA).

Problem 5.4 Let l ≥ 1 and m ≥ 2 be integers, and let SE = (K, E, D) be a given symmetric encryption scheme whose associated plaintext space is {0,1}n, meaning one can only encrypt messages of length n. In order to be able to encrypt longer messages of mn bits, we define a new symmetric encryption scheme SE(m) = (K, E(m), D(m)) having the same key-generation algorithm as that of SE, plaintext space {0,1}mn, and encryption and decryption algorithms as depicted in Fig. 5.11.
(a) Show that AdvSE(m)ind-cca(t, 1, mn, 1, mn) = 1 for some small t.
(b) Show that AdvSE(m)ind-cpa(t, q, mnq) ≤ AdvSEind-cpa(t, mq, mnq) for any t, q.

Part (a) says that SE(m) is insecure against chosen-ciphertext attack. Note this is true regardless of the security properties of SE, which may itself be secure against chosen-ciphertext attack. Part (b) says that if SE is secure against chosen-plaintext attack, then so is SE(m).

disp-quote.p:
algorithm EK(m)(M)
Break M into n-bit blocks M[1],...,M[m]
for i ← 1 to m do
C[i] ← EK(M[i])
return C ← ⟨C[1],...,C[m]⟩
algorithm DK(m)(C)
Break C into n-bit blocks C[1],...,C[m]
for i ← 1 to m do
M[i] ← DK(C[i])
if M[i] = ⊥ then return ⊥
return M ← ⟨M[1],...,M[m]⟩

sec.p: Problem 5.5 The CBC-Chain mode of operation is a CBC variant in which the IV used for the very first message to be encrypted is random, while the IV used for each subsequent encrypted message is the last block of ciphertext that was generated. The scheme is probabilistic and stateful. Show that CBC-Chain is insecure by giving a simple and efficient adversary that breaks it in the IND-CPA sense.
Problem 5.6 Using the proof of Theorem 5.13 as a template, prove Theorem 5.14 assuming Lemma 5.17.

Problem 5.7 Define a notion for indistinguishability from random bits, IND$-CPA. Your notion should capture the idea that the encryption of each message M looks like a string of random bits. Pay careful attention to the number of random bits that one outputs. Then formalize and prove that IND$-CPA security implies IND-CPA security—but that IND-CPA security does not imply IND$-CPA security.
Problem 5.8 Using a game-based argument, prove that CBC$[Func(n, n)] achieves IND$-CPA security. Assume that one encodes ⟨R, C⟩ as R ‖ C.

Problem 5.9 Devise a secure extension to CBC$ mode that allows messages of any bit length to be encrypted. Clearly state your encryption and decryption algorithm. Your algorithm should be simple, should “look like” CBC mode as much as possible, and it should coincide with CBC mode when the message being encrypted is a multiple of the blocklength. How would you prove your algorithm secure?

Your definition should imply IND-CPA security but a scheme meeting your definition can’t be identity-revealing.
